concepts: Differentiation of a determinant
questions.question: If $f(x)=\left|\begin{matrix} x^{3} & 2x^{2}+1 & 1+3x\\ 3x^{2}+2 & 2x & x^{3}+6\\ x^{3}-x & 4 & x^{2}-2\end{matrix}\right|$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, then $2f(0)+f'(0)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The derivative of a determinant is the sum of three determinants, each with one row differentiated.
solution: Differentiate one row at a time: $f'(x)=\left|\begin{matrix} 3x^{2} & 4x & 3\\ 3x^{2}+2 & 2x & x^{3}+6\\ x^{3}-x & 4 & x^{2}-2\end{matrix}\right|+\left|\begin{matrix} x^{3} & 2x^{2}+1 & 1+3x\\ 6x & 2 & 3x^{2}\\ x^{3}-x & 4 & x^{2}-2\end{matrix}\right|+\left|\begin{matrix} x^{3} & 2x^{2}+1 & 1+3x\\ 3x^{2}+2 & 2x & x^{3}+6\\ 3x^{2}-1 & 0 & 2x\end{matrix}\right|$.
The second is $\left|\begin{matrix} 0 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 0\\ 0 & 4 & -2\end{matrix}\right|=0$ (a column of zeros).

alternate_solutions.idea: Keep only terms up to the first power of $x$ in every entry before expanding: $f(x)\approx f(0)+f'(0)x$.
solution: To first order in $x$: row 1 $\approx(0,\,1,\,1+3x)$, row 2 $\approx(2,\,2x,\,6)$, row 3 $\approx(-x,\,4,\,-2)$ (powers $x^{2},x^{3}$ are dropped).

useful_results: If $f(x)=|R_1;R_2;R_3|$ has entries that are functions of $x$, then $f'(x)=\sum_i|\dots R_i'\dots|$ (one row, or one column, differentiated at a time).
To get only $f(0)$ and $f'(0)$ it is enough to expand every entry to first order in $x$ and take the determinant: $f(x)=f(0)+f'(0)x+O(x^{2})$.
A determinant with a zero row or column, or two proportional rows or columns, is $0$ - check this before expanding.
Instance: $f(0)=12$, $f'(0)=18$ here (verified by direct expansion).

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of a piecewise function
Logarithmic differentiation
questions.question: Let $g(x)$ be a linear function and $f(x)=\begin{cases} g(x), & x\le0\\ \left(\dfrac{1+x}{2+x}\right)^{1/x}, & x>0\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=0$. If $f'(1)=f(-1)$, then the value of $g(3)$ is :
questions.key_idea: Continuity at $0$ kills the constant term of $g$; then $f'(1)$ by logarithmic differentiation fixes the slope.
solution: The left limit is $\lim_{x\to0^{-}}(ax+b)=b$, so $b=0$ and $g(x)=ax$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Estimate $g(3)=-3f'(1)$ numerically and eliminate options by size and sign.
solution: Only (A) matches $-1.144$. Same answer (A). (A modest alternative: it still needs $f'(1)$ once.)

useful_results: Piecewise function joined at a point: equate the one-sided limits to the value; this usually fixes a constant (here the intercept of the linear piece).
For $y=u(x)^{v(x)}$: $\frac{y'}{y}=v'\ln u+v\frac{u'}{u}$. Here $v=\frac1x$, $u=\frac{1+x}{2+x}$, which gives the quotient form used above.
$\left(\frac{1+x}{2+x}\right)^{1/x}\to0$ as $x\to0^{+}$ because the base tends to $\frac12<1$ while the exponent tends to $+\infty$.
Instance: $f'(1)=\frac19-\frac23\ln\frac23\approx0.3814$ (checked numerically).

concepts: Differentiation of trigonometric functions
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x-\sqrt2}{\sin x-\cos x}$, $x\in[0,\pi]-\left\{\dfrac\pi4\right\}$. Then $f\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\right)f''\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Write numerator and denominator with the angle $x-\frac\pi4$, so everything depends on one angle.
solution: Since $x+\frac\pi4=(x-\frac\pi4)+\frac\pi2$, the numerator simplifies to $\cos(x-\pi/4)-1$, so $f'(x)=\dfrac{\cos(x-\pi/4)-1}{\sin^{2}(x-\pi/4)}=\dfrac{-(1-\cos(x-\pi/4))}{1-\cos^{2}(x-\pi/4)}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: With $u=x-\frac\pi4$ the function is $\frac{\cos u-1}{\sin u}=-\tan\frac u2$ (half-angle identity); differentiate that.

useful_results: $\dfrac{1-\cos u}{\sin u}=\tan\dfrac u2$, so $\dfrac{\cos u-1}{\sin u}=-\tan\dfrac u2$; spot half-angle forms before using the quotient rule.
$a\sin x+b\cos x=R\sin(x+\varphi)$ with $R=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$: $\sin x\pm\cos x=\sqrt2\sin(x\pm\frac\pi4)$.
If $f=\tan\theta$ (here $\theta=-u/2$), then $f'=\theta'(1+f^{2})$, so higher derivatives come from $f$ alone with no further trigonometry.
Instance: $f=-\frac1{\sqrt3}$, $f''=-\frac{2\sqrt3}{9}$ at $x=\frac{7\pi}{12}$ (checked with sympy).

concepts: Limits using series expansion of cosine
questions.question: The value of $\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{2\left(1-\cos x\sqrt{\cos2x}\sqrt[3]{\cos3x}\cdots\sqrt[10]{\cos10x}\right)}{x^{2}}$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Near $0$, $\cos kx\approx1-\frac{k^{2}x^{2}}2$, so the $k$-th root contributes $1-\frac{kx^{2}}2$.
solution: Write each factor with its expansion: $\cos x\,(\cos2x)^{1/2}(\cos3x)^{1/3}\cdots(\cos10x)^{1/10}\approx\left(1-\frac{x^{2}}2\right)\left(1-\frac{2^{2}x^{2}}2\right)^{1/2}\cdots\left(1-\frac{10^{2}x^{2}}2\right)^{1/10}$.
So the numerator is $2\left[\frac{x^{2}}2(1+2+\cdots+10)\right]=x^{2}\cdot55$ to leading order.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take logarithms: the product becomes a sum $\sum\frac1k\ln\cos kx$, and $\ln\cos t\approx-\frac{t^{2}}2$.

useful_results: $\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{1-\prod_k\cos^{a_k}(b_kx)}{x^{2}}=\dfrac12\sum_ka_kb_k^{2}$ (for finitely many factors): each factor lowers the product by $\frac{a_kb_k^{2}x^{2}}2$.
Here $a_k=\frac1k$, $b_k=k$ gives $\frac12\sum k=\frac{n(n+1)}4$; with the factor $2$ in front the limit is $\frac{n(n+1)}2=55$ for $n=10$.
Cross-terms are $O(x^{4})$ and do not matter; the shortcut works because only the first correction of each factor counts.
Numerical check: $x=10^{-3}$ gives $54.9997\ldots$

concepts: Higher-order derivatives of a polynomial
questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^{3}+x^{2}f'(1)+xf''(2)+f'''(3)$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $f'(10)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $f'(1),f''(2),f'''(3)$ are constants; differentiate three times and set up equations for them.
useful_results: Self-referential polynomial $f=x^{3}+px^{2}+qx+r$ with $p=f'(1)$, $q=f''(2)$, $r=f'''(3)$: differentiate to get a linear system in $p,q,r$. The top-degree derivative is constant, so it is solved first.
Back-substitution check: $f(x)=x^{3}-5x^{2}+2x+6$ gives $f'(1)=-5$, $f''(2)=2$, $f'''(3)=6$, as required.
For $f=x^{n}+\dots$ with constants $f^{(k)}(a_k)$: the $n$-th derivative is the constant $n!$, then work downwards.

concepts: Simplification before differentiation
Differentiation of trigonometric functions
questions.question: If $y=\dfrac{(\sqrt x+1)(x^{2}-\sqrt x)}{x\sqrt x+x+\sqrt x}+\dfrac1{15}\left(3\cos^{2}x-5\right)\cos^{3}x$, then $96\,y'\left(\dfrac\pi6\right)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Factor $x^{2}-\sqrt x$ as a difference of cubes so the first fraction collapses to $x-1$.
solution: The denominator is $x\sqrt x+x+\sqrt x=\sqrt x\left(x+\sqrt x+1\right)$.
Using $(\sqrt x)^{3}-1=(\sqrt x-1)\left(x+\sqrt x+1\right)$, the first term becomes $\dfrac{(\sqrt x+1)\sqrt x(\sqrt x-1)(x+\sqrt x+1)}{\sqrt x(x+\sqrt x+1)}=(\sqrt x+1)(\sqrt x-1)=x-1$.
useful_results: Always simplify before differentiating: $a^{3}-b^{3}=(a-b)(a^{2}+ab+b^{2})$ with $a=\sqrt x$, $b=1$ turns the fraction into $x-1$ (valid for $x>0$).

Trig shortcut: $\dfrac d{dx}\left[\frac{3\cos^{5}x-5\cos^{3}x}{15}\right]=\sin x\cos^{2}x(1-\cos^{2}x)=\sin^{3}x\cos^{2}x$, so $y'=1+\sin^{3}x\cos^{2}x$; at $\frac\pi6$: $1+\frac18\cdot\frac34=\frac{35}{32}$.

concepts: Tangent and normal: geometry of two parabolas
questions.question: The radius of the smallest circle which touches the parabolas $y=x^{2}+2$ and $x=y^{2}+2$ is :
questions.key_idea: The parabolas are mirror images in $y=x$; the circle sits between the nearest pair of points, where both tangents are parallel to $y=x$.
solution: The two parabolas are reflections of each other in the line $y=x$, so the smallest touching circle has its centre on $y=x$ and touches them at mirror points $P$ and $Q$, where the tangents are parallel to $y=x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance of each parabola from the line of symmetry $y=x$: the circle's diameter is twice that distance.
solution: For $y=x^{2}+2$, the points lie above $y=x$ because $x^{2}-x+2>0$ for all $x$; the other parabola is its mirror image, below $y=x$.
Distance of $(x,x^{2}+2)$ from $y=x$ is $\dfrac{x^{2}-x+2}{\sqrt2}$, minimum at $x=\frac12$: $\dfrac{7/4}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{7\sqrt2}8$.
The smallest circle touching both curves has diameter equal to the least gap between them, i.e. twice this distance, $\frac{7\sqrt2}4$.

useful_results: Curves symmetric about $y=x$ (a curve and its inverse relation): the least gap between them is twice the least distance from one curve to $y=x$.
$y=x^{2}+c$ and $x=y^{2}+c$ ($c>\frac14$): smallest touching circle has $r=\dfrac{c-1/4}{\sqrt2}$; $c=2$ gives $\frac{7/4}{\sqrt2}=\frac{7\sqrt2}8$.
At the points of closest approach the common normal is perpendicular to both tangents, so tangents there are parallel.

concepts: Rate of change (related rates)
questions.question: A spherical chocolate ball has a layer of ice-cream of uniform thickness around it. When the thickness of the ice-cream layer is $1$ cm, the ice-cream melts at the rate of $81\ \text{cm}^{3}/\text{min}$ and the thickness of the ice-cream layer decreases at the rate of $\dfrac1{4\pi}$ cm/min. The surface area (in $\text{cm}^{2}$) of the chocolate ball (without the ice-cream layer) is :
questions.key_idea: The chocolate radius $r$ is constant; the outer volume depends on $r+\alpha$ with $\alpha$ the thickness.
solution: Let the ice-cream thickness be $\alpha$ cm and the chocolate radius $r$ (constant). Initially $\alpha=1$.
The ice-cream melts: $\frac{dV}{dt}=-81\ \text{cm}^{3}/\text{min}$, and the thickness decreases: $\frac{d\alpha}{dt}=-\frac1{4\pi}$ cm/min.
Surface area of the chocolate ball $S=4\pi r^{2}=4\pi\cdot64=256\pi$, option (D).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes dV/dt = -81 but then multiplies by +1/(4 pi), dropping the minus sign of d(alpha)/dt. Correct: d(alpha)/dt = -1/(4 pi), so dV/dt = -(r+1)^2 = -81; the magnitude and the answer are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: A thin shell: change in volume $=$ outer surface area $\times$ change in thickness.
solution: The volume lost per minute is the area of the outer surface times the rate at which the thickness shrinks: $81=4\pi R^{2}\cdot\frac1{4\pi}$, where $R=r+1$ is the outer radius.
So $R^{2}=81$, $R=9$ and the chocolate radius is $r=R-1=8$.
Surface area of the chocolate ball $=4\pi\cdot8^{2}=256\pi$. Same answer (D). (This is the usual calculus step in shorter form.)

useful_results: For a sphere $V=\frac43\pi R^{3}$: $\frac{dV}{dt}=S\frac{dR}{dt}$ with $S=4\pi R^{2}$ the surface area; the volume rate is area times the rate of change of the radius.
Quantities held fixed (here the chocolate radius $r$) are constants in the differentiation; only the thickness varies.
Instance: $(r+1)^{2}=81$ gives outer radius $9$ and inner radius $8$.

concepts: Tangent and normal: circle touching a parabola and lines
questions.question: Let $C$ be the circle of minimum area touching the parabola $y=6-x^{2}$ and the lines $y=\sqrt3\,|x|$. Then, which one of the following points lies on the circle $C$ ?
questions.key_idea: By symmetry the centre is on the $y$-axis; the circle meets the lines at $30^{\circ}$ to the axis, so its radius is half the centre's height.
solution: By symmetry the centre lies on the $y$-axis. The circle touches the parabola at its vertex $(0,6)$, so with radius $r$ the centre is $(0,6-r)$ and the circle is $x^{2}+(y-6+r)^{2}=r^{2}$.
The distance from the centre to the line $y=\sqrt3x$ (that is $\sqrt3x-y=0$) must be $r$: $\left|\dfrac{6-r}{2}\right|=r$.
So $6-r=2r$, giving $r=2$. The centre is $(0,4)$ and the circle is $x^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=4$.
Test $(2,4)$: $2^{2}+(4-4)^{2}=4$, so $(2,4)$ lies on the circle. The other options give $(1,2)\to5$, $(2,2)\to8$, $(1,1)\to10$, none equal to $4$.

Note: this is the circle that touches the parabola at the vertex and the lines at $(\pm\sqrt3,3)$; it also cuts the parabola at those two points. The strictly smaller circle $x^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=\frac{k^{2}}4$ with $k=3\sqrt3-2\approx3.196$ lies wholly inside the region, but no option lies on it, so the key (D) refers to the vertex circle above.
questions.correction_note: Answer key (D) kept. The PDF takes the circle touching the parabola at its vertex (centre (0,4), r=2) without saying why; that circle also crosses the parabola at (+-sqrt3,3). A strictly smaller circle tangent to the lines and to the parabola from inside has centre (0,3sqrt3-2) and r=(3sqrt3-2)/2 (about 1.598), but no option lies on it, so (D) is the only consistent choice. A caution bullet was added; the working is otherwise the PDF's.

alternate_solutions.idea: Circle through the three corner points of the region: the vertex $(0,6)$ and the two points $(\pm\sqrt3,3)$ where the lines meet the parabola.
solution: The lines $y=\sqrt3|x|$ meet $y=6-x^{2}$ where $x^{2}+\sqrt3x-6=0$, i.e. $x=\sqrt3$ (for $x>0$): points $(\pm\sqrt3,3)$.
Take the circle with centre $(0,k)$ through $(0,6)$ and $(\sqrt3,3)$: $(6-k)^{2}=3+(3-k)^{2}$, so $36-12k=12-6k$ and $k=4$, $r=2$.

Check: the foot of the perpendicular from $(0,4)$ to $y=\sqrt3x$ is $(\sqrt3,3)$ and the distance is $2=r$, so the circle touches both lines exactly at those points and touches the line $y=6$ (the tangent to the parabola) at $(0,6)$.
The circle is $x^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=4$ and $(2,4)$ lies on it. Same answer (D).

useful_results: A circle with centre $(0,k)$ touching the lines $y=\pm\tan\beta\,x$ has radius $k\cos\beta$; for $y=\pm\sqrt3x$ ($\beta=60^{\circ}$) $r=\frac k2$.
The perpendicular from $(0,k)$ to $y=\sqrt3x$ meets it at $\left(\frac{\sqrt3k}4,\frac{3k}4\right)$; for $k=4$ this is $(\sqrt3,3)$.

Caution: the radius of curvature of $y=6-x^{2}$ at the vertex is $\frac12$, so a vertex-touching circle of radius $2$ crosses the parabola again (at $(\pm\sqrt3,3)$); always check whether 'touching' means tangent at one point or a circle that stays inside.

concepts: Tangent and normal: normals parallel to a given line
questions.question: The number of points on the curve $y=54x^{5}-135x^{4}-70x^{3}+180x^{2}+210x$ at which the normal lines are parallel to $x+90y+2=0$ is :
questions.key_idea: Normal parallel to a line means tangent slope is the negative reciprocal of that line's slope; count the real roots of $y'=90$.
solution: The line $x+90y+2=0$ has slope $-\frac1{90}$, so the normal slope is $m_N=-\frac1{90}$.
Roots: $x=1,\,2,\,-\frac13,\,-\frac23$ - four distinct values of $x$, hence four points on the curve.
Hence there are $4$ such normals, option (C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last line reads '(D) normals', which contradicts both its four roots and the key (C); it should read '4 normals' (option C). Working and answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count sign changes of $9x^{4}-18x^{3}-7x^{2}+12x+4$ with the intermediate value theorem instead of factorising.
solution: Need real roots of $p(x)=9x^{4}-18x^{3}-7x^{2}+12x+4$ (after dividing the equation by $30$). A quartic has at most $4$ real roots.
Sign changes occur in $(-1,-\frac12)$, $(-\frac12,0)$, $(\frac12,\frac32)$ and $(\frac32,3)$: four different intervals, so four distinct real roots.
A quartic cannot have more, so there are exactly $4$ points. Same answer (C).

useful_results: Normal to $y=f(x)$ parallel to $ax+by+c=0$ $\iff$ tangent slope $f'(x)=\dfrac ba$ (the normal slope is $-\frac ab$, the tangent slope is its negative reciprocal). Normal parallel to $x$-axis: $f'=\infty$; tangent parallel to $y=mx$: $f'=m$.
The number of such points equals the number of distinct real roots of $f'(x)=\dfrac ba$ (each root gives one point on the curve).
Counting real roots of a polynomial: if sign changes of $p$ at test points equal the degree, all roots are real and distinct.
Instance: $f'(x)=90$ has roots $1,2,-\frac13,-\frac23$.

concepts: Maximum and minimum of a distance expression (geometric interpretation)
questions.question: Let the maximum and minimum values of $\left(\sqrt{8x-x^{2}-12}-4\right)^{2}+(x-7)^{2}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, be $M$ and $m$ respectively. Then $M^{2}-m^{2}$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Put $y=\sqrt{8x-x^{2}-12}$: the expression is the squared distance from $(7,4)$ to a point of the upper semicircle $(x-4)^{2}+y^{2}=4$.
solution: Squaring: $x^{2}+y^{2}-8x+12=0$, i.e. $(x-4)^{2}+y^{2}=4$, so $P(x,y)$ lies on the upper half of the circle with centre $C(4,0)$, radius $2$.
Hence the expression is $(PQ)^{2}$ where $Q$ is the fixed point $(7,4)$.
Minimum: $CQ=\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}=5$, and the nearest point of the circle (along $CQ$) is in the upper half, so $m=(CQ-2)^{2}=3^{2}=9$.

Maximum: the farthest point of the full circle would lie below the $x$-axis, which is not allowed, so on the upper half the maximum is at the end of the semicircle $(2,0)$: $M=(7-2)^{2}+(4-0)^{2}=25+16=41$ (the other end $(6,0)$ gives only $17$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise the semicircle as $x=4+2\cos\theta$, $y=2\sin\theta$ ($0\le\theta\le\pi$) and reduce to $a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta$.
solution: Minimum is at $\theta=\pi$, value $-5\sin\varphi=-3$ (not $-5$, since $\theta+\varphi$ cannot reach $270^{\circ}$): $E_{\max}=29+12=41$.

useful_results: $\left(\sqrt{R^{2}-(x-h)^{2}}-b\right)^{2}+(x-p)^{2}$ is the squared distance from $(p,b)$ to a point on the upper semicircle; recognise $y=\sqrt{\cdots}$ as a half-circle.
Distance from an outside point $Q$ to a full circle: nearest $(CQ-r)^{2}$, farthest $(CQ+r)^{2}$; for a semicircle check whether those points are in the allowed half, otherwise use the endpoints.
On a restricted angle range, $a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta$ takes its extremes at the interior maximum point or at an endpoint - not automatically $\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$.
Instance: $m=9$, $M=41$.

concepts: Largest circle inscribed in an ellipse (minimum distance from a point)
questions.question: Let $C$ be the largest circle centred at $(2,0)$ and inscribed in the ellipse $\dfrac{x^{2}}{36}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{16}=1$. If $(1,\alpha)$ lies on $C$, then $10\alpha^{2}$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The radius of the largest circle is the least distance from $(2,0)$ to the ellipse, reached where the normal passes through $(2,0)$.
solution: The ellipse is $\frac{x^{2}}{36}+\frac{y^{2}}{16}=1$. A point is $P(6\cos\theta,4\sin\theta)$. The largest circle centred at $(2,0)$ touches the ellipse at the nearest point, where the normal at $P$ passes through $(2,0)$.
Slope of the line from $(2,0)$ to $P$: $\frac{4\sin\theta}{6\cos\theta-2}=\frac{2\sin\theta}{3\cos\theta-1}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $y$: the squared distance from $(2,0)$ to a point of the ellipse is a quadratic in $x$; minimise it.
solution: The vertex of this parabola in $x$ is at $x=\frac{4}{10/9}=\frac{18}5$, inside $[-6,6]$, so it is the minimum.
The largest inscribed circle has $r^{2}=12.8$: $1+\alpha^{2}=12.8$, $\alpha^{2}=11.8$, so $10\alpha^{2}=118$. Same answer.

useful_results: Largest circle centred at $(h,0)$ inside $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$: $d^{2}=\left(1-\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}\right)x^{2}-2hx+h^{2}+b^{2}$, minimised at $x=\frac{ha^{2}}{a^{2}-b^{2}}$ provided this is at most $a$ (i.e. $h\le\frac{a^{2}-b^{2}}{a}$); otherwise the nearest point is the vertex $(a,0)$ and $r=a-h$.

Here $a^{2}-b^{2}=20$, $\frac{ha^{2}}{a^{2}-b^{2}}=\frac{72}{20}=\frac{18}5$ and $r^{2}=b^{2}\left(1-\frac{h^{2}}{a^{2}-b^{2}}\right)=16\cdot\frac45=\frac{64}5$ (formula checked against the direct computation).
A line from the centre of the circle to the point of contact is the common normal.

concepts: Limits of the form 1 to the power infinity
Number of real roots of a cubic
questions.question: Let $f$ be a differentiable function on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $f(2)=1$, $f'(2)=4$. Let $\lim_{x\to0}(f(2+x))^{3/x}=e^{\alpha}$. Then the number of times the curve $y=4x^{3}-4x^{2}-4(\alpha-7)x-\alpha$ meets the $x$-axis is :
questions.key_idea: The limit is of $1^{\infty}$ form, so $\alpha=3f'(2)$; then count the roots of the cubic with the help of its turning points.
solution: It equals $e^{\lim_{x\to0}\frac3x\left(f(2+x)-1\right)}=e^{3f'(2)}$ (the limit in the exponent is a derivative).

The graph rises to a local maximum at $x=-1$ where it only touches the axis, falls to a negative local minimum at $\frac53$, then rises through the axis once more. It meets the $x$-axis at two points, option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Factorise the cubic with the rational-root test: it has a repeated root.
solution: As before, $\alpha=3f'(2)/f(2)=12$ (for $\lim f(2+x)^{k/x}$ with $f(2)=1$, the limit is $e^{kf'(2)}$).
The distinct real zeros are $x=-1$ (double) and $x=3$: exactly two points of intersection with the $x$-axis. Same answer (A).

useful_results: If $\lim f(x)=1$, $\lim g(x)=\infty$, then $\lim f^{g}=e^{\lim g\,(f-1)}$; for $f(a+x)^{k/x}$ with $f(a)=1$ this is $e^{kf'(a)}$.
A cubic with local extreme values $y_1,y_2$ has $3$ real roots if $y_1y_2<0$, exactly $2$ distinct if $y_1y_2=0$ (a double root), and $1$ if $y_1y_2>0$.
The roots of $x^{3}-x^{2}-5x-3$ are $-1,-1,3$ (checked by expansion of $(x+1)^{2}(x-3)$).

concepts: Monotonicity from the sign of the derivative
questions.question: Let the function $f(x)=\dfrac x3+\dfrac3x+3$, $x\ne0$ be strictly increasing in $(-\infty,\alpha_1)\cup(\alpha_2,\infty)$ and strictly decreasing in $(\alpha_3,\alpha_4)\cup(\alpha_4,\alpha_5)$. Then $\sum_{i=1}^{5}\alpha_i^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $f'(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}-9}{3x^{2}}$ changes sign at $\pm3$ and is undefined at $0$.
solution: The denominator $3x^{2}>0$ for $x\ne0$, so the sign of $f'$ is the sign of $(x+3)(x-3)$: positive for $x<-3$, negative on $(-3,0)\cup(0,3)$, positive for $x>3$.
So $f$ is increasing in $(-\infty,-3)\cup(3,\infty)$ and decreasing in $(-3,0)\cup(0,3)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: AM-GM: $\frac x3+\frac3x$ has its minimum at $x=3$ for $x>0$, and $f(x)-3$ is an odd function.
solution: For $x>0$, $\frac x3+\frac3x\ge2$ with equality exactly when $\frac x3=\frac3x$, i.e. $x=3$; as $x\to0^{+}$ and $x\to\infty$ the function tends to $+\infty$, so $f$ decreases on $(0,3)$ and increases on $(3,\infty)$.
$f(x)-3=\frac x3+\frac3x$ is an odd function, so its graph for $x<0$ is the reflection through the origin: increasing on $(-\infty,-3)$, decreasing on $(-3,0)$.
Thus the turning points are $\pm3$ and the break is at $0$, giving $\alpha_i=-3,3,-3,0,3$.

useful_results: $f(x)=px+\dfrac qx$ with $p,q>0$ has turning points at $x=\pm\sqrt{q/p}$: increasing for $|x|>\sqrt{q/p}$, decreasing on $\left(-\sqrt{q/p},0\right)$ and $\left(0,\sqrt{q/p}\right)$. Here $\sqrt{q/p}=\sqrt{9}=3$.
A point where $f$ is undefined (here $x=0$) splits the decreasing set into separate intervals; they cannot be merged into one interval.
Instance: $f(3)=5$ (local minimum) and $f(-3)=1$ (local maximum).

concepts: Monotonicity and intervals of increase/decrease
questions.question: Let $(2,3)$ be the largest open interval in which the function $f(x)=2\log_{e}(x-2)-x^{2}+ax+1$ is strictly increasing and $(b,c)$ the largest open interval in which the function $g(x)=(x-1)^{3}(x+2-a)^{2}$ is strictly decreasing. Then $100(a+b-c)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $f'$ is itself decreasing, so $f$ increases exactly up to the point where $f'=0$; that point is $3$, which fixes $a$.
solution: Since $f$ is increasing exactly up to $x=3$, $f'(3)\ge0$ is needed and the interval $(2,3)$ is the largest only if $f'(3)=0$: $2-6+a=0$, so $a=4$ (for $a>4$ the interval is larger, e.g. $a=5$ gives $\left(2,\frac{9+\sqrt{17}}4\right)$, longer than $(2,3)$).
$g'\le0$ when $(x-2)(5x-8)\le0$ (the factor $(x-1)^{2}\ge0$): sign pattern $+$ for $x<\frac85$ (except $x=1$ where it is $0$), $-$ on $\left(\frac85,2\right)$, $+$ for $x>2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last line reads '100(a+b+c) = 10(4+8/5-2) = 360'. It should be 100(a+b-c) = 100(4+8/5-2) = 360 (the sign of c and the factor 100 were mistyped; the number 360 is right). Working otherwise unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Read $a$ off the numerator of $f'$ (its larger root must be $3$); get $b$ by a section-formula trick for $g$.
solution: $f'(x)=\dfrac{-2x^{2}+(a+4)x-2a+2}{x-2}$. For $x>2$ the sign of $f'$ is the sign of the numerator $N(x)$, a downward parabola, so $f'\ge0$ between its roots.
The interval starting at $2$ ends at the larger root of $N$, so $N(3)=0$: $-18+3(a+4)-2a+2=a-4=0$, giving $a=4$.
For $g=(x-1)^{3}(x-2)^{2}$, $g'=0$ at $x=1,2$ and where $\frac3{x-1}+\frac2{x-2}=0$, i.e. $3(x-2)+2(x-1)=0$, $x=\frac85$ (the weighted point between $1$ and $2$).
Between the stationary points $\frac85$ and $2$ the derivative is negative (e.g. $g'(1.8)<0$), so $g$ decreases exactly in $\left(\frac85,2\right)$.

useful_results: If $f'$ is strictly decreasing (i.e. $f''<0$), then $f$ increases on an interval that ends where $f'$ first becomes $0$; the right end of the 'largest increasing interval' is a root of $f'$.

For $(x-p)^{m}(x-q)^{n}$ with $p<q$, the stationary point between $p$ and $q$ is $x=\dfrac{np+mq}{m+n}$ (it divides $[p,q]$ in the ratio $m:n$ from $p$). Here $\frac{2\cdot1+3\cdot2}5=\frac85$; check on $x(x-1)$: $\frac12$.
The factor with an even power ($(x-1)^{2}$ in $g'$) does not change the sign of $g'$.
Instance: $a=4$, $(b,c)=\left(\frac85,2\right)$.

concepts: Monotonicity: statements on f and f'
questions.question:
For the function $f(x)=\sin x+3x-\dfrac2\pi\left(x^{2}+x\right)$, where $x\in\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]$, consider the following two statements :
(I) $f$ is increasing in $\left(0,\dfrac\pi2\right)$
(II) $f'$ is decreasing in $\left(0,\dfrac\pi2\right)$
Between the above two statements :
questions.key_idea: $f'(x)>0$ follows from $\cos x\ge0$ and a linear lower bound for the remaining part.
solution: Also $\cos x\ge0$ on $\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]$, so $f'(x)>0$ and $f$ is increasing: (I) is true.
$f''(x)=-\sin x-\frac4\pi<0$ for all $x\in\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]$, so $f'$ is decreasing: (II) is true.

alternate_solutions.idea: Do (II) first: $f'$ is decreasing, so its smallest value is at the right end; one evaluation gives (I).
solution: $f''(x)=-\sin x-\frac4\pi<0$ on $\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]$, so $f'$ is decreasing - this proves (II).
A decreasing function has its minimum at the right endpoint: $f'(x)\ge f'\left(\frac\pi2\right)=0+3-\frac2\pi(\pi+1)=1-\frac2\pi\approx0.363>0$.
So $f'>0$ throughout and $f$ is increasing - (I) is true. Same answer (C).

useful_results: If $f''<0$ on an interval then $f'$ is strictly decreasing, so $f'>0$ everywhere on it as soon as $f'>0$ at the right endpoint (and $f'<0$ everywhere as soon as $f'<0$ at the left endpoint).
Bounding technique: separate $f'$ into a bounded trigonometric part ($\cos x\ge0$) and a linear part whose minimum is at an endpoint.
Instance: $f'\left(\frac\pi2\right)=1-\frac2\pi$ is the least value of $f'$ on $\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]$.

concepts: Critical points
questions.question: The number of critical points of the function $f(x)=(x-2)^{2/3}(2x+1)$ is :
questions.key_idea: Critical points are where $f'=0$ or $f'$ does not exist while $f$ is defined: here $x=1$ and $x=2$.
solution: $f'=0$ at $x=1$; $f'$ does not exist at $x=2$ although $f(2)=0$ is defined. Critical points: $1$ and $2$, so there are $2$ critical points, option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $t=(x-2)^{1/3}$ to get a polynomial in $t$ with no fractional powers.
solution: Let $t=(x-2)^{1/3}$ (a one-one map of $\mathbb{R}$ onto $\mathbb{R}$), so $x=t^{3}+2$ and $2x+1=2t^{3}+5$.
$f'=0$ when $t^{3}=-1$, i.e. $x=1$; $f'$ is undefined at $t=0$, i.e. $x=2$.

useful_results: Critical points of $f$: points of the domain of $f$ where $f'(x)=0$ or $f'(x)$ does not exist. Check both kinds, and never count points outside the domain.
For $f(x)=(x-a)^{p/q}g(x)$ with $0<\frac pq<1$, $g(a)\ne0$ and the root real: $x=a$ is a critical point (a cusp or vertical tangent), since $f'$ has a factor $(x-a)^{p/q-1}$.
Instance: $f'$ changes sign from $+$ to $-$ at $x=1$ (local maximum $f(1)=3$) and from $-$ to $+$ at $x=2$ (cusp, local minimum $f(2)=0$).

concepts: Monotonicity and number of roots
questions.question:
For the function $f(x)=\cos x-x+1$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, between the following two statements :
(S1) $f(x)=0$ for only one value of $x$ in $[0,\pi]$.
(S2) $f(x)$ is decreasing in $\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]$ and increasing in $\left[\dfrac\pi2,\pi\right]$.
questions.key_idea: $f'(x)=-(1+\sin x)\le0$ makes $f$ strictly decreasing everywhere, so one sign change means exactly one root.
solution: $f(x)=\cos x-x+1$, so $f'(x)=-\sin x-1=-(1+\sin x)\le0$ for all $x$.
$f'(x)=0$ only at isolated points ($\sin x=-1$), so $f$ is strictly decreasing on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
A continuous strictly decreasing function that changes sign on $[0,\pi]$ has exactly one zero there. (S1) is correct.
(S2) says $f$ increases on $\left[\frac\pi2,\pi\right]$, but $f$ is decreasing everywhere. (S2) is incorrect.

alternate_solutions.idea: Graph view: $\cos x$ decreases on $[0,\pi]$ while the line $x-1$ increases, so they cross at most once.
solution: $f(x)=0\iff\cos x=x-1$. On $[0,\pi]$, $y=\cos x$ is decreasing from $1$ to $-1$ and $y=x-1$ is increasing from $-1$ to $\pi-1$.
A decreasing and an increasing function intersect at most once; at $x=0$ the cosine is above the line ($1>-1$) and at $x=\pi$ below it ($-1<\pi-1$), so they intersect exactly once. (S1) holds.
For (S2): at $x=\frac\pi2$, $f=1-\frac\pi2\approx-0.571$ and at $x=\pi$, $f=-\pi\approx-3.14$; $f(\pi)<f\left(\frac\pi2\right)$, so $f$ does not increase on $\left[\frac\pi2,\pi\right]$. (S2) fails.

useful_results: A strictly monotonic continuous function has at most one zero; a sign change on the interval makes it exactly one (intermediate value theorem).
$f'\le0$ with zeros only at isolated points still gives a strictly decreasing function (no flat stretch).
Equations of the form 'decreasing function $=$ increasing function' have at most one solution.
Instance: $f(0)=2$, $f(\pi)=-\pi$, root near $x\approx1.28$.

concepts: Number of roots of a cubic
Triple-angle formula for cosine
questions.question:
Consider the function $f:\left[\dfrac12,1\right]\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=4\sqrt2x^{3}-3\sqrt2x-1$. Consider the statements :
(I) The curve $y=f(x)$ intersects the $x$-axis exactly at one point
(II) The curve $y=f(x)$ intersects the $x$-axis at $x=\cos\dfrac\pi{12}$.
Then :
questions.key_idea: Recognise $4c^{3}-3c=\cos3\theta$ for $c=\cos\theta$; then use monotonicity on $\left[\frac12,1\right]$ for uniqueness.
solution: So $x=\cos\frac\pi{12}$ satisfies $f(x)=0$; it lies in $\left[\frac12,1\right]$ because $\cos\frac\pi{12}\approx0.966$. Statement (II) is correct.

$f'(x)=12\sqrt2x^{2}-3\sqrt2=3\sqrt2\left(4x^{2}-1\right)\ge0$ for $x\in\left[\frac12,1\right]$, and it is positive for $x>\frac12$ (zero only at the endpoint $x=\frac12$), so $f$ is strictly increasing there.
A strictly increasing function has at most one zero, and $\cos\frac\pi{12}$ is one. So the curve meets the $x$-axis at exactly one point: statement (I) is correct.
questions.correction_note: The PDF says 'Let x = pi/12' and then writes cos 3x; the angle should be called theta (the root is x = cos(pi/12)). It also says f'(x) is positive on [1/2,1], but f'(1/2)=0; it is positive for x>1/2, which still gives strict increase. Neither slip changes the answer (B).

solution: For $x\in\left[\frac12,1\right]$ write $x=\cos\theta$ with $\theta\in\left[0,\frac\pi3\right]$ (cosine is one-one there).
$f=0\iff\cos3\theta=\frac1{\sqrt2}$. Now $3\theta\in[0,\pi]$, where cosine is one-one, so the only solution is $3\theta=\frac\pi4$, i.e. $\theta=\frac\pi{12}$.
Hence there is exactly one root, $x=\cos\frac\pi{12}$. Statements (I) and (II) are both correct. Same answer (B).

useful_results: $4x^{3}-3x=\cos3\theta$ when $x=\cos\theta$ (Chebyshev polynomial $T_{3}$). Any cubic of the form $4x^{3}-3x-c$ with $|c|\le1$ is solved by $x=\cos\frac{\arccos c+2k\pi}3$, $k=0,1,2$ - three real roots.

Here the three roots of $4\sqrt2x^{3}-3\sqrt2x-1=0$ are $\cos\frac\pi{12}\approx0.966$, $\cos\frac{3\pi}4\approx-0.707$, $\cos\frac{17\pi}{12}\approx-0.259$ (each checked in the equation); only the first lies in $\left[\frac12,1\right]$.
The domain restriction $\left[\frac12,1\right]$ is what makes the answer exactly one root: $\theta\in\left[0,\frac\pi3\right]$.
Similarly $3\sin\theta-4\sin^{3}\theta=\sin3\theta$.

concepts: Monotonicity of a rational function
questions.question: The function $f(x)=\dfrac x{x^{2}-6x-16}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}-\{-2,8\}$ :
questions.key_idea: For $f=\frac{x}{x^{2}+bx+c}$ the numerator of $f'$ is $c-x^{2}$, here $-(x^{2}+16)<0$.
solution: For all $x\in\mathbb{R}-\{-2,8\}$ the numerator is negative and the denominator is positive, so $f'(x)<0$.
So $f$ is decreasing on each of the intervals $(-\infty,-2)$, $(-2,8)$, $(8,\infty)$. Option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $f=\dfrac1{h(x)}$ with $h(x)=x-6-\dfrac{16}x$, which is increasing on each side of $x=0$.
solution: At $x=0$ the function is smooth ($f(0)=0$, $f'(0)=-\frac{16}{256}=-\frac1{16}<0$), so there is no break in the decrease across $0$.
Hence $f$ decreases on each interval of its domain. Same answer (A).

useful_results: For $f(x)=\dfrac x{x^{2}+bx+c}$: $f'(x)=\dfrac{c-x^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+bx+c\right)^{2}}$. If $c<0$ then $f'<0$ everywhere and $f$ decreases on every interval of its domain; if $c>0$ then $f$ increases on $\left(-\sqrt c,\sqrt c\right)$ and decreases outside.

A function with 'decreasing' on each interval of the domain is decreasing on the union only in the sense of each interval - it need not be decreasing on the union as a single set (values jump across the poles $x=-2,8$).
